title: Exploring EFL Students’ Prompt Engineering in Human-AI Story Writing: An Activity Theory Perspective
extended_summary:
This paper examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary students decide when and why to prompt generative AI tools while writing short stories. The authors frame the work through Activity Theory and focus on identifying the purposes or conditions governing students’ prompt use, as well as the characteristics of the broader activity systems in which those prompting behaviors occur. The study is not a comparator trial of AI feedback versus other feedback types; instead, it is an exploratory investigation of students’ prompt-engineering practices during human-AI collaborative story writing.

The intervention involved two workshops in Hong Kong secondary schools during the 2022–23 academic year. Students first learned to build their own generative-AI text tools using Python and open-source language models on Hugging Face, then used those tools in a 45-minute short-story writing activity of up to 500 words. Data sources included students’ AI tools, short stories, and responses to an open-ended reflection question about how they decided what words, sentences, or paragraphs to input into the tool. The primary analysis was thematic analysis of the reflections, with additional descriptive examination of story completeness, AI-word use, school academic level, tool sophistication, and rubric-based story quality.

Participants were 67 Hong Kong secondary school students from four schools, spanning Hong Kong secondary grades 1 through 5, which maps roughly onto middle- and high-school levels. The context was school-based workshop/classroom activity in EFL writing. Although the paper includes some rubric-based scoring of story quality by two human experts, it does not test causal effects of generative AI on writing quality against a comparison group.

The authors identify three main prompting themes: unawareness of rules for prompting, prompting to overcome writer’s block, and prompting to develop, expand, or improve the story. They conclude that students vary substantially in metacognitive awareness and strategic use of generative AI, and that teachers should provide tailored scaffolding depending on students’ needs and prompting purposes. The paper argues that better instructional support and tool design could improve human-AI collaboration in EFL writing, but it does not provide direct evidence about effectiveness relative to teacher, peer, self-revision, business-as-usual, or no-feedback comparators.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/mixed descriptive study of 67 secondary students with thematic analysis and descriptive subgroup patterns, but no randomized or quasi-experimental comparator and no causal identification. It meets limited credibility criteria through transparent methods and some inter-coder reliability, but remains below rigorous impact-evaluation standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially beneficial but uneven literacy and metacognitive uses of generative AI in a secondary EFL writing context, yet impact is unclear because there is no direct comparator, no independent-writing outcome, and no reported effect size. Observed associations are descriptive rather than causal.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students built and used open-source generative AI text-generation tools to support short-story writing through prompt engineering, idea generation, elaboration, and story expansion.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined students' short-story writing with generative AI support and qualitatively identified three prompting purposes: unawareness of rules, overcoming writer's block, and developing/expanding/improving the story. Quantitatively, students in the 'overcoming writer's block' group tended to have normal or high rubric-scored writing quality, while the 'unawareness' group tended to score low; however, the paper reports no causal comparison, no pre/post test, and no effect sizes for AI versus non-AI feedback or writing support. Story quality was scored for a subset of 34 students using content, language, and organization rubric ratings by two human experts, but extractable treatment effects are not reported.
finding.measure: Human-expert rubric scores for short-story quality (content, language, organization); story completeness; number of AI-generated words used
finding.study_size: n=67 overall; n=44 shared stories; n=34 stories analyzed under word-limit instructions
finding.std_deviation: reported for categorization thresholds only; exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studied prompt-engineering purposes and metacognitive decision-making during human-AI story writing. Findings suggest some students used AI strategically to overcome writer's block or elaborate pre-existing plans, while a smaller group showed little awareness of when or why to prompt the tool; these patterns indicate variability in students' metacognitive and strategic use of generative AI rather than a measured improvement attributable to the intervention. No effect sizes or causal estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended reflections coded thematically for prompting purposes/conditions; activity-system analysis of tool sophistication and writing context
